newsitem.title: UK: Hard-left leader says single currency needs Italy.
newsitem.headline: Hard-left leader says single currency needs Italy.

text.p: A single European currency without Italian participation would be impossible to implement, the leader of Italy's hard-left Communist Refoundation party said on Friday.
"I don't think it's possible," Bertinotti told reporters during a visit to London, saying it would be unthinkable to exclude one of the world's largest economies from the single currency.

But Bertinotti, whose party holds the balance of power in Italy's lower house of parliament, repeated his opposition to further cuts in public spending to get Italy into shape for the single currency.

The Communist Refoundation leader said those who advocated rigid adherence to the Maastricht Treaty for economic and monetary union (EMU) aspirants were in fact seeking to block the whole single currency project.
He noted that even Germany was struggling to keep its budget deficit within levels currently required for EMU.
Speaking to financiers at a meeting of London's Italian Business Club, Bertinotti said his party supported a single currency but wanted the Maastricht Treaty revised.

Bertinotti said the Maastricht Treaty was flawed in regarding the welfare state purely as a cost and added that the battle to find jobs for the European Union's 20 million unemployed should be made a priority.
A victory for the left in France's forthcoming election would give fresh impetus to the campaign to revise the treaty, he added.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who heads a centre-left coalition, has tied the fate of his government to joining the single European currency in 1999.
Bertinotti, whose party is not a member of the government, denied that his opposition to public spending cuts put him on a collision course with Prodi.

He noted that a series of compromises had been found since Prodi took office a year ago which had resulted in Italy bringing its budget deficit/GDP ratio close to the three percent maximum required by the Maastricht Treaty.
He added that the task was now to find fresh compromises as Italy prepared to grasp the nettle of welfare reform.
"The reform of the welfare state is a fundamental issue but it remains to be seen what sort of reform will be proposed," he said.
Rather than raising taxes, the government should crack down on tax dodging which remained at "unacceptable" levels.
"The taxation issue is really a question of the fight against tax evasion," said Bertinotti.
